text.p: Base metals held up in London overnight but a sharp fall in oil prices and a slump in wheat pushed the CRB Index down to its lowest level since August 1995.

NYMEX crude fell sharply on news rival Kurdish factions agreed to extend a U.S.-brokered ceasefire that ended two months of clashes in northern Iraq, renewing hope for the implementation of an Iraqi oil-for-food deal.
The oil market news, plus a fall in grain prices on fears of a new outbreak of karnal bunt disease, pushed the CRB index 3.75 points lower to 237.91 in late trading.

In late trading on NYMEX, December crude was off $1.03 at $23.25 a barrel, taking the rest of the oil complex down as well. Dealers said crude was testing the area surrounding $23.20 because it represented a 68 percent retracement from the new post-Gulf War high of $26.10 that crude hit earlier in October. Under the oil-for-food deal, the United Nations would have lifted economic sanctions and allowed Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil every six months in exchange for humanitarian aid.

CBOT wheat futures closed unchanged to 9-3/4 cents a bushel lower on reports of karnal bunt fungus in Tennessee and on world that the EU had riased its wheat export subsidy. Traders said talk of karnal bunt had raised fears that U.S. wheat could be rejected by importers.

Copper prices turned tail above $1,970 during late afternoon LME trading on Thursday, with profit-taking and technical selling persuading speculative buyers to hold their fire. Nevertheless the market still concluded a fairly active session in the plus column, and is in good shape for another attempt on the $1,970 level and above in coming days.
"All the ingredients are in place - stocks should be down, the spreads are tight, and there is option covering on time decay to be done," one trader said.

Warehouse stock data will be of paramount importance on Friday, with the general expectation being a decline of some 5,000/10,000 tonnes. However, the current impressive run of drawdowns may be nearing an end, as some of the metal shipped from Europe is expected to land in Singapore soon.

"The jury is still out on whether the (stock) falls are consumption or just relocation. It could be some time before we find out, because the Chinese figures (import/export) will not show for a month or so," another trader said.
Final three months business on the kerb was at $1,958, an $8 a tonne advance from Wednesday's closing kerb.

Elsewhere, zinc prices relinquished highs near $1,070 resistance, with the market in need of a breather after a run-up towards five-month highs. But the short-term outlook remains bright, given current fund interest, notably the perception that international financier George Soros has a market presence now.
Also, there are expectations of a fall in warehouse stocks on Friday, as well as some late-January 1997 tightness.
Final trade was at $1,066, up $12 from the overnight close.

Aluminium stumbled at the $1,450 hurdle in mid-afternoon, having earlier ridden higher in copper's slipstream through the $1,440 level. In the short term traders still favour a foray towards $1,500, but movements will be choppy. Last trade today was at $1,437, still up $9 from yesterday's kerb.
Nickel struggled to make much headway throughout the session and mostly held close to overnight levels. Final kerb business was at $7,330, against Wednesday's close of $7,340.
Lead's upside flurry petered out during the afternoon, with prices drifting back from the highs to close at $752, still up $4 from yesterday and a technically sound finish.

COMEX December gold ended down $2.20 at $379.10, after seeing a life-of-contract low at $377.70 intraday, with commodity funds seen probing the downside. In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $377.50/378.00 an ounce, compared to the London Thursday afternoon fix at $379.50 and the New York close Wednesday at $380.15/380.55.
